title: A surjective flat closed immersion of algebraic spaces is an isomorphism
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], let $X,Y$ be algebraic spaces over $S$ [def-trf-algebraic-space] in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention], and let $i:X\to Y$ be a morphism. Suppose that $i$ is flat in the chartwise sense of [def-sfb-space-morphism-properties], that $|i|:|X|\to|Y|$ is surjective on the point sets of [def-a1-space-point-topology], and that $i$ is a closed immersion: it is representable and every scheme base change $X\times_YT\to T$ is a closed immersion of schemes [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Then $i$ is an isomorphism of algebraic spaces. Fibre products are the sheaf fibre products of [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers]. No finite-presentation, reducedness or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 05XD (spaces-more-morphisms-lemma-where-isomorphism), proof, final paragraph: representable surjective flat closed immersion; scheme input Tag 04PW (morphisms-lemma-characterize-flat-closed-immersions) in literature/stacks-project/morphisms.tex.

proof.text: Choose a representable surjective etale scheme atlas $p:h_U\to Y$. The pullback $W=X\times_Yh_U$ is a scheme and $j:W\to U$ is a closed immersion by the hypothesis on $i$. Its other projection $h_W\to X$ is etale by the fibre-product lemma. Thus $j$ is one of the chart tests in the definition of flatness, so $j$ is flat. Since $i$ is representable and $|i|$ is surjective, the point-calculus lemma says that every scheme base change of $i$, in particular $j$, is surjective.

source.place: Tag 05XD (lemma-where-isomorphism), proof, final paragraph; chart and sheaf details expanded using spaces.tex Tag 0262 (lemma-space-presentation).

proof.text: Apply the scheme lemma to $j$: it is an isomorphism. For any $S$-scheme $T$ and $y\in Y(T)$, the atlas local-lifting lemma gives an fppf cover $v:V=T\times_YU\to T$ with a map $a:V\to U$ over $y$. The fibre of $X(V)\to Y(V)$ over $y|_V$ is a singleton: its representing scheme $X\times_YV$ identifies with $W\times_UV$, and the inverse of $j$ gives the unique section of its projection to $V$. The identification sends $(x,z)$ to $(x,a(z),z)$; its inverse forgets the middle coordinate.

source.place: Tag 05XD (lemma-where-isomorphism), proof, final paragraph; chart and sheaf details expanded using spaces.tex Tag 0262 (lemma-space-presentation).

proof.text: For $x,x^{\prime}\in X(T)$ with common image $y$, take the cover $V\to T$ of the preceding step. Uniqueness of its lift gives $x|_V=x^{\prime}|_V$. The uniqueness part of the sheaf equalizer for $X$ then gives $x=x^{\prime}$. Hence $i_T:X(T)\to Y(T)$ is injective for every $T$.

source.place: Tag 05XD (lemma-where-isomorphism), proof, final paragraph; chart and sheaf details expanded using spaces.tex Tag 0262 (lemma-space-presentation).

proof.text: For $y\in Y(T)$, let $x_V$ be its unique lift on the cover in step 2. On $V\times_TV$ its two restrictions have the same image; injectivity from step 3 makes them equal. The sheaf equalizer for $X$ glues them to $x\in X(T)$. Its image equals $y$ since their restrictions agree on $V$ and $Y$ is a sheaf. Thus each $i_T$ is bijective. The inverses are natural: restriction of a lift is a lift of the restricted section and is unique by step 3. They therefore define a morphism $Y\to X$ inverse to $i$.
